query: Consider the following context: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. In that context, which method can be used for calculate its melting properties, including the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using a two‐phase coexistence method that simulates a solid–liquid interface in a DFT (or DFT‐augmented with ML potentials) framework can reliably predict the melting temperature, as well as the entropy and enthalpy of fusion and the volume change at the melting point for refractory materials, with lower computational cost compared to full thermodynamic integration.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory material in its stable solid phase with a known crystalline structure
generation.intervention: Set up a DFT-based (or DFT-guided with machine-learning potentials) molecular dynamics simulation cell that contains both the crystalline (solid) and disordered (liquid) phases, allowing them to equilibrate under constant pressure and varying temperatures.
generation.conditions: High temperature conditions relevant to melting in refractory substances, under controlled pressure and simulation settings that minimize finite-cell effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The solid–liquid interface established within the simulation cell, which mediates energy and structural exchange between phases.
generation.mechanism: At the equilibrium where both phases coexist, the system naturally exhibits a plateau in temperature; analysis of energy, volume, and entropy changes across the interface allows extraction of melting properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The simulation will reveal a clear temperature plateau corresponding to the melting transition, and by analyzing the changes at the interface, one can extract melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and the volume change at melting that are in qualitative (and approximately quantitative) agreement with experimental data and more expensive full free-energy integration methods.
generation.baseline: Previous ab initio free-energy methods using full thermodynamic integration by ab initio molecular dynamics, which are computationally intensive.
generation.boundary: This method is expected to work well when the simulation cell is large enough to host a well-defined interface and when ML potentials (if used) are accurately trained on DFT data; limitations may appear for materials with very subtle interface effects or when finite-size effects are pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: While qualitative trends are expected, quantitative differences may arise due to finite-size effects, inaccuracies in potential fitting (if ML potentials are employed), and the inherent approximations of DFT. The exact margin of error in predictions is uncertain without further benchmarking against experimental data.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct two-phase coexistence simulations on a refractory material using DFT-based MD (or DFT-guided ML potentials). Initiate the simulation with coexisting solid and liquid regions and allow equilibration. Measure the steady-state temperature plateau and record the changes in energy, entropy, and volume as the system transitions from solid to liquid. Compare these results with experimental data and results from full thermodynamic integration.
measurements: Melting temperature from the temperature plateau
Enthalpy and entropy of fusion derived from energy differences
Volume change at the melting point
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the melting temperature and the derived thermodynamic quantities from the two-phase coexistence simulation differ by more than about 10–15% from results obtained by experimental measurements or high-accuracy thermodynamic integration, the hypothesis that this approach is a computationally efficient and sufficiently accurate alternative would be falsified.
